topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which type of ownership exists when a single person or legal entity holds title to real property alone, with no co-owners?
explanation: Ownership by one person or entity alone, without any co-owners, is called ownership 'in severalty' (sole ownership) -- the owner's interest is 'severed' from any other owner's interest.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'estate in severalty'; standard real estate principles texts (e.g., Modern Real Estate Practice).

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: The 'four unities' of time, title, interest, and possession must all be present at creation for which form of co-ownership?
explanation: A joint tenancy requires the four unities (PITT: Possession, Interest, Time, Title) -- co-owners must acquire equal, undivided interests at the same time, by the same document, with equal rights of possession. Its hallmark is the right of survivorship.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'joint tenancy'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: In a joint tenancy, when one joint tenant dies, what happens to that tenant's ownership interest?
choice_a: It passes according to the deceased tenant's will
choice_b: It passes to the deceased tenant's heirs under intestate succession
choice_c: It passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s) by right of survivorship, outside of probate
choice_d: It is divided equally between the deceased tenant's estate and the surviving tenants
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy is the right of survivorship: a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically and immediately to the surviving joint tenant(s), bypassing the deceased's will and probate estate entirely.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'right of survivorship'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which form of co-ownership is generally available only to married couples (or, in some states, registered domestic partners), and prevents a creditor of only one spouse from attaching the property?
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of co-ownership limited to married couples, includes right of survivorship, and generally protects the property from a creditor pursuing only one spouse individually. It is not recognized in every state.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'tenancy by the entirety'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Two unrelated business partners take title to a commercial building together without specifying a form of ownership and without survivorship language. Absent other facts, most states will presume they hold title as:
explanation: Tenancy in common is the default/presumed form of co-ownership when the deed does not clearly create a joint tenancy. Tenants in common may hold unequal, undivided interests, there is no right of survivorship, and each owner's interest passes to their own heirs or devisees.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts; Cornell LII Wex, 'tenancy in common'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: In community property states, property acquired by either spouse during the marriage (other than by gift or inheritance) is generally treated as owned:
choice_a: Entirely by whichever spouse earned or purchased it
choice_b: Equally by both spouses, regardless of whose name appears on title
choice_c: By the state until the marriage ends
choice_d: As tenants in common in unequal shares based on income
explanation: Under the community property system used in a minority of U.S. states, most property acquired during the marriage is owned equally by both spouses; property owned before the marriage, or received individually by gift or inheritance, generally remains separate property.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'community property'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which of the following best describes a 'fee simple absolute' estate?
choice_a: An ownership interest that lasts only for the life of the owner
choice_b: An interest that automatically terminates if a stated condition occurs
choice_c: The greatest, most complete ownership interest recognized by law, of potentially infinite duration and subject to no private conditions (only to government powers such as taxation, eminent domain, police power, and escheat)
choice_d: A right to occupy land for a fixed term of years
explanation: Fee simple absolute is the highest form of ownership -- freely inheritable, transferable, and of unlimited duration, limited only by the four government powers (taxation, eminent domain, police power, escheat), not by any private condition.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'fee simple'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A deed conveys land 'to the City, so long as the land is used as a public park.' What estate is created, and what happens if the City stops using the land as a park?
choice_a: Fee simple subject to condition subsequent; the grantor must exercise a right of re-entry
choice_b: A life estate; the land reverts only upon the death of the grantor
choice_c: Fee simple absolute; there is no risk of forfeiture
choice_d: Fee simple determinable; title reverts automatically to the grantor (or the grantor's heirs) under a possibility of reverter
explanation: Durational language such as 'so long as,' 'while,' or 'during' creates a fee simple determinable. If the stated condition is violated, title reverts automatically to the grantor by operation of the grantor's retained possibility of reverter -- no lawsuit or re-entry is needed.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'fee simple determinable' and 'possibility of reverter'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A deed states: 'to Buyer, but if alcohol is ever sold on the premises, Grantor may re-enter and terminate the estate.' What estate does this create?
choice_a: Fee simple subject to condition subsequent, with the grantor retaining a right of re-entry (power of termination)
choice_d: A life estate pur autre vie
explanation: Conditional language such as 'but if,' 'provided that,' or 'on condition that' creates a fee simple subject to condition subsequent. Unlike a fee simple determinable, title does not revert automatically -- the grantor holds a right of re-entry (power of termination) that must be affirmatively exercised to end the estate.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'fee simple subject to condition subsequent' and 'right of entry'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A grants a life estate 'to B, for the life of C.' If C dies while B is still alive, B's estate ends immediately even though B is living. This is an example of:
choice_b: A life estate pur autre vie
explanation: A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant -- here, C -- is a life estate 'pur autre vie' (French for 'for the life of another'). B's interest ends when the measuring life, C, ends.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'life estate pur autre vie'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: When a life estate ends, the property may be designated to pass to a third party named in the original conveyance, rather than back to the original grantor. That third party's future interest is called a:
explanation: If the future interest following a life estate returns to the original grantor (or the grantor's heirs), it is a 'reversion.' If it is instead granted to a third party named in the conveyance, it is a 'remainder,' and that party is a 'remainderman.'
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'remainder' and 'reversion'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A life tenant strips valuable timber from the land for personal profit and allows the improvements to fall into serious disrepair, substantially reducing the property's value for the person who holds the remainder interest. This conduct is legally known as:
explanation: A life tenant has a legal duty not to injure the interests of the remainderman or reversioner. Conduct that unreasonably damages or depletes the property's value, such as stripping resources or allowing it to deteriorate, constitutes 'waste' and can give rise to a legal claim by the future interest holder.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'waste'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which statement best describes the 'bundle of rights' concept of real property ownership?
choice_a: Ownership consists of a set of separate legal rights -- such as the rights of possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment, and disposition -- any of which can be separated from the bundle and transferred or encumbered individually
choice_b: Ownership is a single, indivisible right to occupy land
choice_c: It refers only to the physical improvements attached to land
choice_d: It refers exclusively to the rights held by a mortgage lender
explanation: The 'bundle of rights' metaphor describes real property ownership as a collection of distinct legal rights (possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment, disposition) that can be separated -- for example, an owner can lease out the right of possession, or grant an easement affecting the right to exclude, while retaining the rest of the bundle.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts (e.g., Modern Real Estate Practice); widely used foundational concept in U.S. real property law.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A tenant leases retail space for a fixed five-year term that ends on a specific stated date, with no automatic renewal. No notice to vacate is required because the leasehold terminates automatically on that date. This describes a(n):
explanation: An estate for years has a definite, agreed-upon beginning and ending date (it need not actually be a year in length) and terminates automatically at the end of the stated term without either party needing to give notice.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'estate for years' / 'tenancy for years'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A month-to-month residential tenancy that automatically renews for successive periods until either party gives the legally required notice to terminate is an example of a(n):
explanation: A periodic tenancy (e.g., month-to-month or year-to-year) automatically renews for successive periods until one party gives proper advance notice of termination, unlike an estate for years, which simply expires on its stated end date.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'periodic tenancy'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A tenant remains in possession after the lease term has expired, without the landlord's consent, but the landlord has not yet taken legal action to remove the tenant. This holdover possession is best classified as a(n):
explanation: An estate at sufferance arises when a tenant's original possession was lawful but continues without the landlord's permission after the leasehold ends. It is what distinguishes a holdover tenant from a trespasser, whose original entry onto the land was never lawful.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'tenancy at sufferance'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A leasehold with no fixed term and no automatic renewal, which either the landlord or the tenant may terminate at any time (subject to any notice required by law), is called a(n):
explanation: An estate (tenancy) at will has no fixed duration and continues only as long as both landlord and tenant agree; either party may terminate it. It also generally ends automatically upon the death of either party or a transfer of the property.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'tenancy at will'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: In a 'gross lease,' who is generally responsible for paying the property's operating expenses, such as property taxes, insurance, and maintenance?
choice_a: The tenant, in addition to the base rent
choice_b: The landlord, out of the rent collected
choice_c: The expenses are automatically split 50/50 between landlord and tenant
choice_d: Neither party -- the expenses are waived
explanation: Under a gross lease (common in many residential leases), the tenant pays a fixed rent amount, and the landlord is responsible for paying the property's operating expenses out of that rent.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts, lease classification terminology.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A commercial lease requires the tenant to pay a base rent plus some or all of the property's operating expenses (such as taxes, insurance, and/or maintenance) separately from the rent. This is best described as a:
explanation: In a net lease, the tenant pays a base rent plus some or all of the operating expenses directly or through additional charges. Variants (net, net-net, triple net) refer to how many expense categories -- taxes, insurance, maintenance -- the tenant assumes.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts, commercial lease classification terminology.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A shopping-center tenant pays a base rent plus a percentage of the store's gross sales once sales exceed a stated 'breakpoint.' This describes a:
explanation: A percentage lease, common for retail tenants, combines a base (minimum) rent with an additional rent calculated as a percentage of the tenant's gross sales above an agreed breakpoint amount.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts, commercial lease classification terminology.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: What is the key legal difference between a 'general lien' and a 'specific lien'?
choice_a: A general lien attaches to all of a debtor's property, real and personal, while a specific lien attaches only to a particular, identified property
choice_b: A general lien is always voluntary and a specific lien is always involuntary
choice_c: A general lien can only be created by a court judgment, while a specific lien can only arise by contract
choice_d: There is no meaningful legal difference between them
explanation: A general lien (e.g., a judgment lien or an IRS tax lien) attaches to all of a debtor's property within the jurisdiction; a specific lien (e.g., a mortgage or a mechanic's lien) attaches only to the particular property identified in connection with the debt.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'lien'; standard real estate principles texts on general vs. specific liens.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which of the following is a voluntary lien?
explanation: A mortgage (or deed of trust) lien is voluntary because the property owner agrees to grant it as security for a loan. Mechanic's liens, tax liens, and judgment liens are all involuntary -- imposed by law, a contractor, or a court without requiring the owner's consent.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'lien'; standard real estate principles texts on voluntary vs. involuntary liens.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: As a general rule, when two or more liens are recorded against the same property, priority among them is determined by:
choice_a: The dollar amount of each debt, with the largest debt taking priority
choice_b: Whether the lienholder is a bank rather than an individual
choice_c: The order in which the liens were recorded -- 'first in time, first in right'
choice_d: Alphabetical order of the lienholders' names
explanation: The general rule for lien priority is 'first in time, first in right' -- liens are typically paid in the order they were recorded, with earlier-recorded liens taking priority over later-recorded ones, subject to specific statutory exceptions.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'lien priority'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which type of lien is a well-established exception to the general 'first recorded, first in priority' rule, typically taking superpriority even over an earlier-recorded mortgage?
choice_b: A mechanic's lien for work performed after the mortgage was recorded
choice_d: An ad valorem (general real property) tax lien
explanation: General real property tax liens are a recognized exception to the 'first in time' priority rule: they generally take superpriority status ahead of previously recorded liens, including mortgages, reflecting the government's priority claim for unpaid property taxes.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'tax lien'; standard real estate principles texts on lien priority exceptions.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A contractor who performs work on real property but is not paid can record what type of lien against that specific property to secure payment?
explanation: An unpaid contractor, subcontractor, or material supplier can file a mechanic's (or construction) lien against the specific property that was improved, to secure payment for labor or materials provided.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'mechanic's lien'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: The right to occupy and use the space above the surface of a parcel of land -- which can be severed from the underlying land and sold or leased separately, such as for a structure built over an existing building or for transferable development rights -- is known as:
explanation: Air rights are the rights to use and control the airspace above a parcel of land. They can be severed from the surface estate and separately sold, leased, or transferred (for example, as transferable development rights in urban areas).
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'air rights'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Mineral rights beneath the surface of a parcel of land may be severed from surface ownership and conveyed to a different owner. This severance is generally accomplished by:
choice_c: A mineral deed, or a reservation of mineral rights within a deed
explanation: Subsurface (mineral) rights can be separated from the surface estate through a mineral deed conveying them to another party, or through a reservation clause in a deed by which the grantor keeps the mineral rights while conveying the surface.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts on surface, subsurface, and mineral rights.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which of the following is generally required for a deed to be legally valid between the grantor and grantee?
choice_a: It must be recorded in the county land records
choice_b: The grantee must sign the deed
choice_c: It must be witnessed by a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: A legally competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, a granting clause (words of conveyance), an adequate legal description, and the grantor's signature, along with delivery and acceptance
explanation: A valid deed generally requires: a grantor with legal capacity, a named/identifiable grantee, words of conveyance (granting clause), an adequate legal description of the property, and the grantor's (not the grantee's) signature, plus delivery of the deed with intent to convey and acceptance by the grantee. Recording is not required for the deed to be valid between the parties -- it primarily protects priority against later purchasers and creditors.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'deed'; standard real estate principles texts on elements of a valid deed.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Title to real property actually passes from grantor to grantee at the moment of:
choice_a: Delivery of the deed by the grantor with intent to convey title, and acceptance of the deed by the grantee
choice_b: Recording of the deed in the public records
explanation: Title passes upon valid delivery of the deed by the grantor, with intent that it take effect, and acceptance by the grantee. Recording is not what transfers title -- it establishes constructive notice to the public and protects the grantee's priority against later claims.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'delivery'; standard real estate principles texts on deed delivery and acceptance.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A deed contains a full set of title covenants -- including covenants of seisin, the right to convey, against encumbrances, quiet enjoyment, warranty forever, and further assurances -- under which the grantor warrants title against defects arising both during and before the grantor's own period of ownership. This is a:
explanation: A general warranty deed provides the greatest protection to a grantee: the grantor warrants and defends title against all claims, whether arising before or during the grantor's ownership, through its full set of title covenants.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'warranty deed' and 'covenant'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A special warranty deed differs from a general warranty deed in that the grantor warrants title only:
choice_a: For ten years after the closing date
choice_b: If the buyer also purchases title insurance
choice_c: Against defects and encumbrances arising during the grantor's own period of ownership, not before
choice_d: Against defects caused by the buyer after the transfer
explanation: In a special (limited) warranty deed, the grantor warrants and defends title only against claims and defects arising during the time the grantor owned the property -- not against defects that may have existed before the grantor acquired title.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'special warranty deed'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor actually holds in the property (if any), contains no covenants or warranties of title, and is commonly used to clear a cloud on title. This is a:
explanation: A quitclaim deed conveys only the grantor's present interest, if any, with no warranties or guarantees about the quality or validity of that title. It is often used to release a possible claim and clear a cloud on title, such as between family members or former spouses.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'quitclaim deed'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which of the following best describes a 'bargain and sale deed'?
choice_a: It implies that the grantor holds title to the property but includes no express covenants or warranties against encumbrances
choice_b: It contains a full set of title covenants like a general warranty deed
choice_c: It conveys no ownership interest at all
choice_d: It can be used exclusively to convey mineral rights
explanation: A bargain and sale deed implies (without expressly stating) that the grantor holds title and the right to convey it, but does not contain express covenants or warranties defending against encumbrances or defects, unlike a warranty deed.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts on deed types.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: The transfer of title by a property owner's own free act -- such as by executing and delivering a deed, or by leaving property to heirs through a will -- is known as:
explanation: Voluntary alienation is the transfer of title at the owner's own choice, such as by deed during life (a sale or gift) or by will/devise at death.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'alienation'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which of the following is an example of involuntary alienation of title?
choice_a: A homeowner sells their house and signs a deed to the buyer
choice_b: A homeowner transfers property to their child by gift deed
choice_c: A lender forecloses on a defaulted mortgage and title passes at a foreclosure sale
choice_d: A homeowner leaves the property to a beneficiary in a will
explanation: Foreclosure, eminent domain (condemnation), escheat, tax sales, and adverse possession are all forms of involuntary alienation -- transfers of title that occur by operation of law, without (or against) the current owner's consent.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'alienation'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: When a property owner dies intestate (without a will) and no heirs can be located or identified, title to the property passes to the state through the process of:
explanation: Escheat is the process by which property reverts to the state when an owner dies intestate leaving no ascertainable heirs, ensuring property never remains permanently without an owner.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'escheat'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A person openly occupies another's land, treating it as their own, continuously and exclusively without the true owner's permission for the statutory period required by state law, and may eventually acquire legal title through:
explanation: Adverse possession generally requires possession that is open and notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile (without the owner's permission) for a statutory period, which varies by state; if the requirements are met, the possessor may gain legal title.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'adverse possession'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Recording a deed in the public land records gives all subsequent parties, and the world at large, legal notice of its contents, whether or not they actually examined the records. This is known as:
explanation: Constructive notice is notice imputed by law to everyone once a document is properly recorded in the public records, regardless of whether a particular party actually looked at or knew about it.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'constructive notice'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A prospective buyer personally inspects a property before purchase and observes a tenant physically living there. Even though nothing about the tenancy has been recorded, the buyer has what type of notice of the tenant's possible rights?
explanation: Actual notice is real, personal, direct knowledge of a fact -- such as seeing a tenant in possession -- as opposed to constructive notice, which is imputed by law from the recorded public records.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'actual notice'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: The complete history of every recorded document and legal proceeding affecting title to a specific parcel of land, traced from the earliest available record forward to the present owner, is known as the:
explanation: The chain of title is the complete, unbroken chronological sequence of every recorded conveyance and legal proceeding affecting ownership of a particular parcel, from the earliest available record to the present.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'chain of title'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A condensed written summary of the chain of title, listing all recorded conveyances, liens, and other encumbrances affecting a specific parcel, is called a(n):
explanation: An abstract of title is a condensed history -- a written summary -- of all the recorded documents and proceedings affecting title to a specific parcel, compiled from the public records.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'abstract of title'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Title that is reasonably free from the risk of litigation over its validity, and free of defects, liens, or encumbrances that a reasonably prudent buyer would object to, is described as:
explanation: Marketable title is title that a reasonably prudent, informed buyer would be willing to accept -- free of defects, encumbrances, or defects in the chain of title that would expose the buyer to litigation or an unreasonable risk of loss.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'marketable title'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: An unreleased old mortgage still showing in the public record, a competing claim by an undisclosed heir, or a forged deed somewhere in the chain of title are all examples of a:
explanation: A cloud on title is any document, claim, unreleased lien, or other irregularity of record that appears to impair title or casts doubt on its validity, even if it ultimately proves to be invalid or unenforceable.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'cloud on title'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A lawsuit filed to remove a cloud on title and establish clear, marketable ownership of record is called a(n):
explanation: A quiet title action is a lawsuit brought to resolve competing claims to real property and remove a cloud on title, resulting in a court judgment that establishes clear ownership.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'quiet title action'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Before closing, a buyer may obtain a formal written opinion from a real estate attorney, based on examination of the abstract of title, addressing whether title appears marketable. This is known as:
explanation: An attorney's opinion of title is the attorney's written conclusion, based on review of the abstract of title and public records, as to the state of title and whether it appears marketable -- one traditional alternative (or supplement) to purchasing title insurance.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts on methods of evidencing title (attorney opinion, title insurance, Torrens registration).

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: An owner's title insurance policy primarily protects the property owner against:
choice_a: Future changes to local zoning ordinances
choice_b: Financial loss from title defects that existed but were not disclosed by the public records search, such as forgery, fraud, or undisclosed heirs
choice_c: Physical damage to the structure from fire or storms
choice_d: Declines in the property's market value
explanation: Title insurance protects against losses from defects in title that existed at the time of purchase but were not uncovered by the title search -- such as forged prior deeds, undisclosed heirs, or recording errors -- unlike a hazard insurance policy, which covers physical damage to the property.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'title insurance'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: In a typical residential purchase financed with a mortgage loan, who is generally required to purchase a lender's (mortgagee's) title insurance policy?
choice_c: The buyer/borrower, to protect the lender's security interest in the property
explanation: Lenders typically require the borrower to purchase a lender's (mortgagee's) title insurance policy, which protects the lender's security interest up to the loan amount; this is separate from, and does not substitute for, an owner's policy protecting the buyer's equity.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts on owner's vs. lender's title insurance policies.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Which statement about a deed of trust used as a financing/security instrument is most accurate?
choice_a: It conveys the property directly and permanently to the lender as owner
choice_b: It eliminates the need for a promissory note
choice_c: It can only be used to finance commercial property
choice_d: It involves three parties -- the borrower (trustor), the lender (beneficiary), and a neutral third-party trustee who holds legal title or a power of sale as security for repayment of the loan
explanation: A deed of trust is a three-party security instrument: the borrower (trustor) conveys title, or a lien interest, to a neutral trustee, who holds it for the benefit of the lender (beneficiary) as security for the loan evidenced by a promissory note. Some states use deeds of trust and others use mortgages as the security instrument for real estate loans.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'deed of trust'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: In a condominium form of ownership, what does an individual unit owner typically hold?
choice_a: Fee simple title to the individual unit's interior airspace, plus an undivided tenancy-in-common interest, together with the other unit owners, in the building's common elements and the underlying land
choice_b: A sole fee simple interest in the entire building, including every other owner's unit
choice_c: Only a renewable annual leasehold interest in the unit
choice_d: Shares of stock in a corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease to the unit
explanation: A condominium owner holds fee simple title to their individual unit (typically defined as interior airspace) and, together with the other unit owners, an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the building's common elements (land, structure, hallways, roof, etc.). This differs from a cooperative, where the 'owner' actually holds stock plus a proprietary lease.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'condominium'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: In a cooperative form of ownership, what does an individual 'owner' actually hold?
choice_a: Fee simple title to the unit plus a tenancy-in-common interest in the common elements
choice_b: Shares of stock in the cooperative corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit
choice_c: Direct fee simple ownership of the entire building
choice_d: A life estate in the unit, measured by the life of the corporation's president
explanation: A cooperative 'owner' does not own real property directly. Instead, the corporation owns the building, and the resident owns shares of stock in that corporation plus a proprietary lease (an occupancy agreement) granting the right to occupy a specific unit -- a personal property and leasehold interest, not a real property fee interest.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'cooperative' (housing cooperative); standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Co-tenants (such as joint tenants or tenants in common) who cannot agree on the use or sale of their jointly held property, and cannot voluntarily agree to divide their interests, may ask a court to physically divide the property or, if that is impractical, order it sold with the proceeds divided among them. This remedy is called a(n):
explanation: A partition action is a judicial proceeding available to co-tenants who cannot agree on disposition of jointly owned property. The court may physically divide the property (partition in kind) or, more commonly when division is impractical, order a sale and distribute the proceeds according to each co-tenant's ownership share.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'partition'; standard real estate principles texts on co-tenancy remedies.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: One of three joint tenants sells and conveys their interest in the property to an outside buyer, without the consent of the other two joint tenants. What is the legal effect of this conveyance?
choice_a: The conveyance is void because a joint tenant cannot transfer their interest without the unanimous consent of the other joint tenants
choice_b: The joint tenancy remains fully intact, and the buyer simply steps into the seller's shoes as a joint tenant with full survivorship rights
choice_c: The property automatically converts to community property
choice_d: The joint tenancy is severed as to that interest; the buyer takes ownership as a tenant in common with the remaining owner(s), and the right of survivorship no longer applies to that share
explanation: A joint tenant may unilaterally convey their own interest without the other joint tenants' consent, but doing so destroys the unities of time and title as to that interest and severs the joint tenancy for that share. The buyer becomes a tenant in common with whatever joint tenancy (or tenancy in common) remains among the others, and survivorship no longer applies to the conveyed share.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'joint tenancy' (severance); standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Under a 'race-notice' recording statute, a later bona fide purchaser for value who takes without notice of an earlier, unrecorded conveyance will prevail over the earlier grantee only if the later purchaser also:
choice_a: Also records their own deed before the earlier conveyance is later recorded
choice_b: Pays a higher price for the property than the earlier grantee paid
choice_c: Takes physical possession of the property before the earlier grantee does
choice_d: Purchases an owner's title insurance policy
explanation: A race-notice recording statute protects a subsequent purchaser only if that purchaser (1) took without notice of the prior unrecorded conveyance AND (2) records their own deed first, before the earlier conveyance is recorded. This combines the 'race' element (first to record wins) with the 'notice' element (must be a bona fide purchaser without notice), unlike pure race statutes or pure notice statutes.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'recording statutes' (race-notice statute).

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: What is the Torrens system, as used for evidencing title in a limited number of U.S. jurisdictions?
choice_a: A type of adjustable-rate mortgage instrument
choice_b: A government-administered system of land title registration in which the state examines title and issues a certificate of title guaranteed by the government, used as an alternative to relying on chain-of-title searches and title insurance
choice_c: A federal program that insures lenders against losses on FHA-insured loans
choice_d: A standardized method of writing metes-and-bounds legal descriptions
explanation: The Torrens system is a government-run title registration system, adopted in only a handful of U.S. jurisdictions, in which the state examines and registers title and issues a certificate of title that is conclusively guaranteed -- functioning as an alternative to the traditional chain-of-title search plus title insurance model used almost everywhere else.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Torrens system'; standard real estate principles texts on methods of evidencing title.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: An easement that benefits one specific parcel of land (the dominant estate), burdens an adjacent parcel (the servient estate), and automatically transfers with the dominant estate whenever it is sold, is called a(n):
choice_a: Easement in gross, which benefits a specific person or company rather than a parcel of land
choice_b: License, which is a revocable personal privilege
choice_d: Encroachment, an unauthorized physical intrusion onto a neighbor's land
explanation: An easement appurtenant runs with the land: it benefits a dominant estate and burdens a servient estate, and automatically passes to new owners of the dominant parcel when it is sold, without needing to be separately mentioned. This contrasts with an easement in gross, which benefits a particular person or entity rather than another parcel of land.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'easement appurtenant'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A neighbor openly and continuously uses a footpath across another's land, without permission, for the full statutory period required by state law. Rather than acquiring ownership of that strip of land, the neighbor instead acquires a permanent right merely to continue using it, known as a(n):
choice_a: Adverse possession claim, which would transfer full ownership of the strip of land
choice_b: License, which remains revocable at the landowner's will
choice_c: Reversion, which returns automatically to the original grantor
explanation: An easement by prescription arises from open, continuous, and adverse use of another's land for the statutory period, similar to adverse possession -- but it grants only a permanent right to use that portion of the servient land for the specific purpose exercised, not title/ownership of the land itself.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'easement by prescription'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A homeowner gives a neighbor oral permission to cross the homeowner's yard as a shortcut. The permission can be revoked by the homeowner at any time and does not bind a future buyer of the yard. This is best described as a(n):
choice_a: License -- a personal, revocable privilege to use the land that is not an interest in real property and does not run with the land to future owners
choice_b: Easement appurtenant that automatically transfers with the property when it is sold
choice_c: Easement in gross that binds all future owners of the servient land
choice_d: Profit a prendre entitling the neighbor to remove soil or timber from the yard
explanation: A license is merely a personal, revocable privilege to use another's land for a specific purpose. Unlike an easement, it is not an interest in real property, is generally revocable at the will of the landowner, and does not run with the land to bind subsequent owners.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'license' (real property); standard real estate principles texts distinguishing a license from an easement.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Landowner A's property borders a flowing river, and Landowner B's property borders a non-flowing natural lake. Landowner A holds ___ rights in the adjacent water, and Landowner B holds ___ rights.
explanation: Riparian rights belong to landowners bordering flowing waterways such as rivers and streams. Littoral rights belong to landowners bordering non-flowing bodies of water such as lakes, seas, and oceans. Both concern an owner's rights to use and access adjacent water, but the terms apply to different types of water bodies.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'riparian rights' and 'littoral rights'.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Over many years, a river gradually and imperceptibly deposits soil along a landowner's bank, slowly enlarging the parcel. This process -- and the landowner's resulting gain of title to the newly formed land -- is called:
explanation: Accretion is the gradual, imperceptible buildup of soil deposited by water action along a landowner's boundary, and the landowner generally acquires title to the newly formed land. This differs from avulsion (a sudden, perceptible change in a watercourse or shoreline, which generally does not shift the boundary), erosion (gradual loss of land), and reliction (land permanently exposed as water recedes).
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'accretion'; standard real estate principles texts on water boundary changes (accretion, avulsion, erosion, reliction).

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A landowner leases raw or improved land to a tenant for a long term -- often 50 to 99 years -- under which the tenant typically constructs and owns improvements on the land during the lease term. This is best described as a:
explanation: A ground lease is a long-term lease of the land itself (often 50 to 99 years), under which the tenant commonly finances and constructs improvements and owns them during the lease term; ownership of the improvements may revert to the landowner when the ground lease ends, depending on the lease terms.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts, lease classification terminology (ground lease).

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: Under an installment land contract (contract for deed), the seller retains legal title until the buyer completes all payments called for in the contract. In the meantime, what interest does the buyer hold?
choice_a: Equitable title and the right of possession, while the seller retains legal title until the contract is paid in full
choice_b: Full legal title immediately upon signing, identical to a cash purchase
choice_c: No ownership interest of any kind until the final payment is made
choice_d: A leasehold estate only, terminable at the seller's will
explanation: In an installment land contract (contract for deed), the seller keeps bare legal title as security for the unpaid purchase price, while the buyer takes possession and holds equitable title -- the beneficial ownership interest -- during the contract term. Legal title transfers to the buyer only once all payments required by the contract have been made.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'installment land contract' / 'contract for deed'; standard real estate principles texts.

topic: Forms of Ownership, Transfer, and Recording of Title
question: A retail tenant installs custom shelving, attaching it to the wall for use in the business. In deciding whether the shelving became a fixture (real property) rather than remaining personal property, courts primarily look to:
choice_a: Only the item's dollar value or replacement cost
choice_b: The method and permanence of the item's attachment to the real property, its adaptation to the property's use, and the intent of the party who installed it
choice_c: Only who paid the property taxes for the year the item was installed
choice_d: Only the physical size and weight of the item
explanation: The common-law test for whether an item has become a fixture looks primarily at (1) the method and permanence of attachment to the real property, (2) the item's adaptation to the use of the property, and (3) the intent of the party who installed it -- not simply its cost, size, or unrelated facts such as who paid taxes that year.
source_note: Standard real estate principles texts, common-law fixtures test (method of attachment, adaptation, intent).
